title: Epidemiology and Public Health
bigQuestion: How can studying whole groups of people help keep each person healthy?

story.title: A Town Signs Up
story.kicker: In 1948 thousands of neighbors in one Massachusetts town agreed to let doctors study their hearts for life.
paragraphs: In the late 1940s, heart disease was the leading cause of death in the United States. Doctors could describe a heart attack. But they could not say why some people had one at 50 while others lived heart-healthy lives into old age. Many thought hardening of the arteries was simply part of getting older.

The U.S. Public Health Service decided to watch a whole community over many years. It chose Framingham, Massachusetts, a town west of Boston. In 1948 researchers began signing up adults. The first group grew to about 5,200 men and women, aged about 30 to 62. None had yet had a heart attack or stroke.

Every two years or so, the volunteers came in for a checkup. Researchers measured blood pressure, weight and cholesterol. They asked about smoking and exercise. Then they waited. Over the years, some volunteers developed heart disease. Researchers looked back at what those people had in common.

Clear patterns appeared. People with high blood pressure, high cholesterol or a smoking habit were more likely to develop heart disease. The Framingham team helped make the term risk factor common in medicine. Later, the children and grandchildren of the first volunteers joined the study too.

Framingham showed the power of a new way of thinking. By studying a whole population patiently, doctors could find causes they could never see in a single patient. That kind of study is the heart of this chapter.
story.think: Why did researchers need to follow people for years instead of just checking them once?

lessons.title: New Cases and All Cases
lessons.mainIdea: Incidence counts new cases over a time; prevalence counts all current cases at one moment.
reading: The science of how diseases spread and affect groups of people is called *epidemiology*. Its first job is counting. Epidemiologists ask how many people are sick, where they live and when they got sick. Two counts matter most. The first is how many new cases appear. The second is how many people have a condition right now.

*Incidence* is the number of new cases in a group over a set time, such as new flu cases in Illinois during one week. It tells you how fast a disease is appearing. A sudden jump in incidence is often the first sign of an outbreak. Health departments watch incidence closely for this reason.

*Prevalence* is the number of people who have a condition at one point in time, whether they got it last week or ten years ago. Long-lasting conditions like diabetes can have high prevalence even if incidence is steady, because people live with them for years.

Think of a bathtub. Incidence is the water flowing in from the tap. Prevalence is the water already in the tub. Recovery and death are the drain. A good treatment that helps people live longer can actually raise prevalence, because fewer people leave through the drain.

words.d: the study of how diseases spread and affect groups of people
the number of new cases of a disease in a group during a set time
the number of people who have a condition at one point in time

look.title: The Bathtub Model
look.text: A school has 600 students. In October, 30 students catch a stomach bug, and each is sick for about three days. In the same school, 12 students have asthma, a long-lasting condition, and none were newly diagnosed in October.
look.prompt: For each condition, is it better described by high incidence or high prevalence in October? Explain using the bathtub model.

check.q: What does incidence measure?
choices: All people who have ever had a disease
New cases in a group during a set time
The number of doctors in a city
check.why: Incidence counts new cases over a period, like the water flowing in.

check.q: Why can diabetes have high prevalence even with steady incidence?
choices: People live with it for many years
It only lasts a few days
check.why: Long-lasting conditions build up in a population, so prevalence stays high.

check.q: In the bathtub model, what does the drain stand for?
check.why: People leave the prevalence pool by recovering or dying, like water leaving through the drain.

lessons.title: Outbreak, Epidemic, Pandemic
lessons.mainIdea: An outbreak, epidemic and pandemic differ mainly in how widely a disease spreads.
reading: An *outbreak* is more cases than expected in a limited place, such as a school or a town. In 1854, a cholera outbreak struck the Soho area of London. The doctor John Snow mapped the deaths and found they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. His work helped show that cholera spreads through dirty water.

An *epidemic* is a bigger rise in cases across a larger area, such as a country. A *pandemic* is an epidemic that spreads across many countries and continents. The words describe how far a disease spreads, not how deadly it is. A mild disease can cause a pandemic, and a deadly one can stay a small outbreak.

The 1918 influenza pandemic spread around the world in waves. The CDC estimates that about 500 million people were infected, roughly a third of the world's population then. At least 50 million died. There were no flu vaccines or antibiotics for the lung infections that often followed.

In 2020, the World Health Organization described COVID-19, caused by a new coronavirus, as a pandemic. It spread quickly through air travel and close contact. Scientists worldwide shared data and developed vaccines within about a year. Each pandemic has taught public health workers new lessons about preparing.

words.d: more cases of a disease than expected in a limited place
a large rise in cases of a disease across a wide area, such as a country
an epidemic that spreads across many countries and continents

check.q: What did John Snow find in 1854?

check.q: What makes a pandemic different from an epidemic?
choices: A pandemic is always more deadly
A pandemic spreads across many countries and continents
A pandemic lasts only one week

lessons.title: A Long Epidemic: HIV
lessons.mainIdea: HIV was first recognized in 1981, and research turned it from a usually fatal illness into a manageable one for many people.
reading: In June 1981, the CDC published a short report about five young men in Los Angeles with a rare lung infection. Their immune systems were not working well. Doctors soon saw more cases. The illness was named *AIDS*, short for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.

By 1984, scientists had identified the cause: a virus later named *HIV*, the human immunodeficiency virus. HIV attacks cells of the immune system. It spreads through certain body fluids, such as blood. It does not spread through hugs, sharing a desk or touching a doorknob.

For years there was no effective treatment. Then, in the mid-1990s, doctors began combining several medicines at once. This *antiretroviral therapy* keeps the virus under control. It does not cure HIV. But many people who take it every day can live long, healthy lives and have children.

HIV became a worldwide epidemic, hitting parts of Africa especially hard. UNAIDS and the World Health Organization track it across the globe. Public health work on testing, treatment and prevention continues. Anyone with questions can talk privately with a doctor, nurse or school nurse.

words.d: the human immunodeficiency virus, which attacks cells of the immune system
acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, the advanced stage of untreated HIV infection
a combination of medicines that keeps HIV under control but does not cure it

look.title: Myth or Fact?
look.text: Three students talk. Ana says you can get HIV from sharing a water fountain. Ben says HIV medicines can keep the virus under control for many years. Cal says HIV medicines cure the infection completely.
look.prompt: Which student is correct? Use the reading to explain what is wrong with the other two statements.

check.q: When did the CDC first report the illness later called AIDS?
check.why: The CDC's first report on these cases was published in June 1981.

check.q: Which statement about antiretroviral therapy is true?
choices: It cures HIV in a week
It keeps HIV under control but does not cure it
It is a vaccine given at birth
It only works on the flu
check.why: Combination therapy controls the virus so people can live long lives, but it is not a cure.

check.q: Which of these does NOT spread HIV?
choices: Sharing needles with blood on them
Blood from an infected person entering a cut
check.why: The reading says HIV does not spread through hugs, sharing a desk or touching a doorknob.

lessons.title: Tracing Contacts
lessons.mainIdea: Contact tracing finds people exposed to an infection so they can get tested, treated or stay home.
reading: Imagine a student is diagnosed with measles. Measles spreads very easily through the air. Public health workers call the family. They ask where the student has been and who they were near in the days before getting sick. This process is called *contact tracing*.

Each person identified is a *contact*. Workers reach out to the contacts, explain the risk and check whether they are protected, for example by vaccination. Some may be asked to stay home for a set time, called *quarantine*, to see if they get sick without spreading it further.

Contact tracing is old but powerful. It has been used for tuberculosis, sexually transmitted infections, Ebola and COVID-19. It works best when cases are caught early and people trust health workers enough to share information. Each new case that is caught early can prevent several more.

Tracing depends on privacy. Health workers do not tell contacts the name of the sick person. Protecting privacy helps people feel safe cooperating. That trust is one of public health's most important tools. Contacts also get clear, calm advice about what to watch for and whom to call.

words.d: finding people who were near a sick person so they can be checked
a person who was near someone with an infection
staying away from others after an exposure to see if illness develops

look.title: A Tracing Call
look.text: A health worker calls a family. She says: Someone your son sat near at a practice last Tuesday has an illness that spreads through the air. I can't share who it is. Has your son had his shots? Please watch for fever and a rash for the next two weeks, and call us if you see them.
look.prompt: Find two things the worker does that build trust. Why might keeping the sick person's name private help the whole community?

check.q: What is the main goal of contact tracing?
choices: To find people exposed so they can be checked and stop further spread
check.why: Tracing finds contacts early so they can be tested, protected or stay home.

check.q: What is quarantine?
choices: Staying away from others after exposure to see if illness develops
check.why: Quarantine keeps possibly exposed people apart while waiting to see if they get sick.

check.q: Why do tracers keep the sick person's name private?
choices: Because the law bans all phone calls
check.why: Privacy builds the trust that makes people willing to share information.

lessons.title: What Framingham Found
lessons.mainIdea: A risk factor raises the chance of a disease; the Framingham Heart Study found several for heart disease.
reading: The Framingham Heart Study began in 1948 and still continues. It is a *cohort study*: researchers pick a group of people, called a cohort, and follow them over time. Because they measure people before anyone gets sick, they can see what came first. That order matters when you want to find causes.

Over years of checkups, patterns emerged. Volunteers with high *blood pressure* were more likely to have heart attacks and strokes. So were people with high *cholesterol*, a fatty substance in the blood, and people who smoked. Later findings added lack of exercise, diabetes and obesity.

Each of these is a *risk factor*: something that raises the chance of a disease. A risk factor is not a guarantee. Many smokers never have a heart attack, and some nonsmokers do. But across thousands of people, the pattern is clear. It raises the odds for a group, but it does not decide what happens to one person.

These findings changed medicine. Doctors began checking blood pressure and cholesterol at routine visits. They started talking with patients about smoking and exercise. Heart disease is still common, but U.S. death rates from it have fallen a great deal since the 1960s, thanks to prevention and better treatment.

words.d: a study that follows a chosen group of people over time
something that raises the chance of getting a disease
the force of blood pushing on the walls of the arteries
a fatty substance in the blood; high levels can clog arteries

look.title: The Study Describes Itself
look.text: The Framingham Heart Study describes its goal as identifying the common factors that contribute to heart and blood vessel disease, by following a large group of people who had not yet developed symptoms or suffered a heart attack or stroke.

choices: A cohort study that follows people over time
check.why: Framingham follows a chosen group of people over many years.

check.q: What is a risk factor?
choices: Something that raises the chance of a disease
A disease that spreads through water
check.why: A risk factor raises the chance but does not guarantee the disease.

check.q: Which was NOT one of Framingham's early heart disease risk factors?
check.why: The reading lists blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking; glasses are not a risk factor.

lessons.title: Smoking and Lung Cancer
lessons.mainIdea: Studies in the 1950s by Doll and Hill and others showed that smoking causes lung cancer.
reading: In the early 1900s, lung cancer was rare. By the 1940s, doctors in Britain and the United States were seeing far more of it. Some blamed car exhaust or road tar. Two British researchers, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill, set out to find the cause.

In 1950 they published a *case-control study*. They interviewed patients with lung cancer, the cases, and similar patients in the same hospitals without it, the controls. Nearly all the lung cancer patients smoked, and heavy smokers were most at risk. In the United States, Ernst Wynder and Evarts Graham reported similar findings the same year.

Doll and Hill then began a cohort study. From 1951 they followed tens of thousands of British doctors and their smoking habits. Smokers died of lung cancer far more often than nonsmokers. The more they smoked, the higher the risk. Doctors who quit lowered their risk.

The evidence met Hill's clues for causation: strong, repeated, dose-related and with the cause coming first. In 1964, the U.S. Surgeon General's report concluded that smoking causes lung cancer in men. Smoking rates in the United States have fallen greatly since then.

words.d: a study that compares people with a disease to similar people without it
when more exposure leads to a bigger effect
the leading public health official of the U.S. government

choices: Compared lung cancer patients with similar patients without it
Randomized people to smoke or not smoke
check.why: Their 1950 case-control study compared cases with lung cancer and controls without it.

check.q: What group did Doll and Hill follow in their cohort study from 1951?
check.why: They followed tens of thousands of British doctors and their smoking habits.

check.q: What did the 1964 U.S. Surgeon General's report conclude?

check.why: The 1964 report concluded that smoking causes lung cancer in men.

lessons.title: Watching Over Health
lessons.mainIdea: The CDC and the WHO track diseases and help communities respond, at home and around the world.
reading: When a new illness appears, someone has to notice, count and respond. In the United States, that job falls largely to the *CDC*, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It began in Atlanta in 1946, first working to control malaria in the South.

The CDC gathers reports from state and local health departments, such as the Illinois Department of Public Health and the Chicago Department of Public Health. This steady watching for disease is called *surveillance*. It helps spot outbreaks early. The CDC also studies injuries, chronic diseases and environmental health.

Diseases do not stop at borders. The *WHO*, the World Health Organization, was founded in 1948 as part of the United Nations. It helps countries share data, sets health guidelines and coordinates responses to global threats. April 7, the day its constitution took effect, is marked as World Health Day.

Neither agency can do everything alone. They depend on local nurses, doctors, labs and ordinary people who report illness and follow guidance. Public health is a team effort, from a school nurse to an international agency. Everyone who washes hands, stays home when sick or reports an illness is part of it.

words.d: the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the main U.S. public health agency
the World Health Organization, the United Nations agency for health, founded in 1948
steady watching and counting of diseases to spot problems early

look.prompt: Why does each level need to share information? What might happen if the clinic did not report?

check.q: When and where did the CDC begin?
check.why: The reading says the CDC began in Atlanta in 1946.

check.q: What is disease surveillance?
choices: Steady watching and counting of diseases to spot problems early

check.q: What is the WHO part of?
check.why: The WHO was founded in 1948 as part of the United Nations.

lessons.title: Ending Smallpox
lessons.mainIdea: Vaccination and careful surveillance made smallpox the first human disease ever eradicated.
reading: Smallpox was a disease caused by a virus. It caused fever and a rash of blisters. For thousands of years it killed or scarred many millions of people. In 1796, the English doctor Edward Jenner showed that material from cowpox, a mild related disease, could protect people. This was an early *vaccine*.

A vaccine trains the immune system to recognize a germ without causing the full disease. When enough people in a community are protected, a disease has trouble spreading. This is called *herd immunity*. It also shields people who cannot be vaccinated, such as very young babies.

In 1967 the WHO began an intensified campaign to end smallpox. Vaccinating everyone everywhere was not possible. So teams used a strategy called ring vaccination: find each case, then vaccinate the people around it. Surveillance and contact tracing made this work.

The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977. In 1980 the WHO declared smallpox *eradicated*, gone from nature worldwide. It remains the only human disease to be eradicated. Health workers are working to do the same for polio. Polio cases have fallen by more than 99 percent since the late 1980s.

words.d: a substance that trains the immune system to protect against a germ
protection for a whole community when enough people are immune
completely removed from nature everywhere in the world

look.title: The Ring Around a Case
look.text: A health team hears of a smallpox case in a village. They isolate the sick person. They list everyone in the household and nearby homes. They vaccinate all of those people and watch them for signs of illness. Then they move on to the next reported case.
look.prompt: Why might this ring strategy work better than trying to vaccinate an entire country at once?

check.q: What did Edward Jenner show in 1796?
choices: That cowpox material could protect against smallpox
check.why: Jenner used cowpox material to protect against smallpox, an early vaccine.

check.q: What is herd immunity?
choices: Protection that only farm animals have
Protection for a community when enough people are immune
check.why: When enough people are immune, a disease struggles to spread, protecting others too.

check.q: In what year did the WHO declare smallpox eradicated?
check.why: The last natural case was in 1977, and eradication was declared in 1980.

lessons.title: Where We Live Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Social determinants, like housing, income and schools, shape health as much as medical care does.
reading: Two children live a few miles apart. One lives near parks and grocery stores with fresh food. The other lives near a busy highway, with few stores selling fresh food and older housing. Their doctors may be equally good. But their health chances may differ.

The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age are called *social determinants of health*. They include income, education, housing, safe neighborhoods, clean air and water, and access to care. The WHO and the CDC both use this idea.

Researchers have found that life expectancy can differ by years between neighborhoods in the same city, including Chicago. These gaps are called *health disparities*. Their causes are debated. Most researchers point to several factors working together, such as income, pollution, access to care and past policies about where people could live.

Public health tries to improve conditions for everyone. Examples include removing lead paint from old homes, adding clinics where few exist, and improving school meals. Choices about how to do this, and who should pay, are often debated in politics. But the goal is shared: a healthy start for every person.

words.d: the conditions where people live, learn, work and age that shape their health
differences in health between groups of people
the average number of years people in a group are expected to live

look.text: The World Health Organization describes social determinants of health as the non-medical factors that influence health: the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live and age, and the wider forces and systems shaping daily life.

check.why: Housing is one of the living conditions that shape health.

choices: Differences in health between groups of people

lessons.title: Public Health Choices
lessons.mainIdea: Public health measures protect groups, but people debate how to balance safety, freedom and cost.
reading: Many things we take for granted came from public health work. Clean tap water, sewers, seat belts, food inspections and smoke-free indoor spaces all prevent illness or injury for whole populations. Most people never notice the diseases that did not happen.

Some measures ask something of individuals. Examples include school vaccine requirements, smoking bans and, during COVID-19, rules about masks and closures. Supporters say these protect the vulnerable and the whole community. Critics say some go too far into personal choice, or cost too much for families and businesses.

These are real debates about values as well as facts. Evidence can show what a measure does. It cannot alone decide how to weigh safety against freedom or cost. Communities decide that through elected leaders, courts and public discussion. Knowing the difference between a fact question and a values question helps everyone discuss health calmly.

Good public health leaders explain their reasoning, share data openly and change guidance when new evidence arrives. That honesty builds *public trust*. When you hear health advice, you can ask what the evidence shows, who it protects and what it costs.

words.d: work that protects and improves the health of whole communities
the confidence people have that health leaders are honest and fair
all the people in a group or place being studied or served

look.title: Two Views
look.text: View 1: A city should ban smoking in all restaurants because secondhand smoke harms workers who cannot easily avoid it. View 2: Owners should decide for their own restaurants, and customers can choose where to eat.
look.prompt: What evidence could each side use? What values does each side care most about?

check.q: Which is an example of a public health measure?
check.why: Clean water protects the health of whole populations.

check.q: Why are some public health rules debated?

check.why: Evidence shows what a measure does, but people disagree on how to weigh values.

check.q: What helps health leaders build public trust?
